subject: A few things I noticed about German Autowerke's online presence
body:
Hi Vincent,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across German Autowerke and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- You're ahead of most shops out here — online appointment booking and a 5-star review section right on the homepage. That's exactly the right instinct.
- Genuinely excellent reputation (Yelp 125, Birdeye 322 at 4.9) and 35+ years of German-marque specialization.

Where you're leaving money on the table
- No after-hours capture. You're closed evenings and all weekend, so a Porsche or BMW owner who finds you Saturday has the booking button but no human and no instant callback — high-ticket inquiries that cool off by Monday.
- No live chat. A lot of customers want a quick "can you work on my Audi?" answer before they commit to booking.
- Your Google setup is incomplete behind the scenes — the page only has a basic address block, not the full LocalBusiness markup (hours, location, service type) that tells Google to surface you for "BMW repair near me" searches. You're likely ranking below shops doing worse work.

None of this is urgent, and your reputation clearly speaks for itself — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

Best,
Leo Lebel
cheddar.lebel@gmail.com

subject: A few things I noticed about EXP Auto Repair's online presence
body:
Hi Hamid,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across EXP Auto Repair and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- You've got more dialed in than most shops here — an appointment request form, a free-estimate offer, Saturday hours, and the full behind-the-scenes Google markup (LocalBusiness/AutoRepair schema) already in place. Nicely done.
- Solid reputation (Yelp 86, positive sentiment).

Where you're leaving money on the table
- Your reputation is invisible on your own site. You point people off to leave a review, but a visitor deciding between you and the next shop sees no testimonials on the homepage itself. Pulling those onto the site is a cheap, high-leverage win.
- No live chat. A lot of younger customers won't call — they'll ask a quick question in a chat box or leave.
- Your contact email is a generic gmail.com address. Beyond looking less established, those can hurt deliverability when you email customers — worth a branded address on your own domain.
- No instant after-hours capture. The form is good, but there's no automated callback catching a lead while they're still deciding at night.

None of this is urgent, and the shop clearly runs well — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

subject: A few things I noticed about Subie Shop's online presence
body:
Hi there,

I run a small studio that helps local auto and performance shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Subie Shop and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- Clear niche (Subaru / Japanese performance), a branded email, two testimonials on the site, and full LocalBusiness schema with your hours — that's better setup than most shops out here.
- Strong off-site reputation (SureCritic 4.9 across 159, Yelp 73).

Where you're leaving money on the table
- No real online booking. There's a contact form, but no actual scheduling widget — so a Subaru owner ready to lock in a slot has to wait for a callback instead of booking on the spot.
- No after-hours capture. Your hours are tight (closed Friday afternoon and all weekend), which is exactly when enthusiasts are thinking about their builds — and right now those inquiries sit until you reopen.
- No live chat for the quick "can you tune my WRX?" questions that turn into booked work.
- Most of your 150+ reviews live off-site. You've got two on the homepage — surfacing more of that reputation where people are actually deciding is a cheap win.

None of this is urgent, and your reputation clearly speaks for itself — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.
